misconceptions.description: The student thinks that a BST stays balanced whatever the insertion order, so search is always O(log n).
misconceptions.appResponse: The student builds a chain in C2, and the step counter shows n comparisons.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why does sorted input turn a BST into a chain, and what does that do to search?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that the shape of a BST does not depend on the order in which the keys are inserted.
misconceptions.appResponse: The app shows two trees side by side, built from the same keys in two orders (A D E F Z and E A D F Z).
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: How does the insertion order decide the shape of a BST?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that any insertion order that is not sorted gives a balanced BST.
misconceptions.appResponse: The app shows a zig-zag order (1, 7, 2, 6, …) that builds a chain of the same height as sorted input.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Which insertion orders give a tall BST, apart from sorted ones?

misconceptions.description: The student confuses the worst case with the average case.
misconceptions.appResponse: The feedback separates the worst case, which is a search to the bottom of the chain, from an average search.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: What is the difference between worst-case and average-case cost for BST search?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that an AVL tree stays balanced by sorting the keys before inserting them.
misconceptions.appResponse: C5 opens with the point from the slides that rebuilding from sorted data is expensive, and that rotations avoid this cost.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: How do rotations keep a tree balanced without sorting the data first?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that an AVL tree can still become a chain, for example with sorted input.
misconceptions.appResponse: The C2 preview and the C6 challenge insert sorted keys into an AVL tree, and the result is a balanced tree.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: What stops an AVL tree from becoming a chain when keys arrive in sorted order?

misconceptions.description: The student counts nodes instead of edges when finding a height.
misconceptions.appResponse: The feedback counts the edges on the path, and the conventions card shows that a leaf has height 0.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why does the course count height in edges, so that a leaf has height 0?

misconceptions.description: The student gives an empty branch a height of 0, or confuses a leaf with an empty branch.
misconceptions.appResponse: The feedback restates that an empty branch has height −1, which is one less than a leaf.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why is the height of an empty subtree −1?

misconceptions.description: The student uses h(left) − h(right) for the balance factor, so the sign is reversed.
misconceptions.appResponse: The feedback restates bf = h(right) − h(left) with the node's own numbers.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Which sign convention does the lecture use for balance factors, and what does a negative value mean?

misconceptions.description: The student checks the balance only at the root.
misconceptions.appResponse: The app shows “Spot the problem” trees in which the root is balanced but a node lower down is not.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why must the AVL rule hold at every node, not just at the root?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that “balanced” means that every level is full, or that the height is exactly log₂ n.
misconceptions.appResponse: The app shows valid AVL trees that are not full, and it explains that requiring equal heights everywhere would be too rigid.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why does the AVL rule allow a height difference of 1 instead of requiring equal heights?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that AVL search uses balance factors to choose a path.
misconceptions.appResponse: The pseudocode has no balance-factor step, and a caption explains that balance only limits the length of the path.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: If search ignores balance factors, how does balance make search faster?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that a search visits every node, or both branches, like a traversal.
misconceptions.appResponse: The trace highlights a single path, and the step counter stays at or below height + 1.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why does a search follow only one path from the root?

misconceptions.description: The student stops a search before it reaches the key or an empty branch, for example as soon as the key is smaller than a node.
misconceptions.appResponse: The pseudocode panel shows that a smaller key means “go left”, not “stop”.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: When exactly does a search stop?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that the most comparisons a search can need equals the height, which is one too few.
misconceptions.appResponse: The step counter shows height + 1 comparisons for the deepest key.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why can a search need height + 1 comparisons rather than height?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that an in-order traversal lists the keys in insertion order or level by level.
misconceptions.appResponse: The in-order check before and after each rotation lists the keys in sorted order.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why does an in-order traversal of a BST give the keys in sorted order?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that a rotation can break the BST order.
misconceptions.appResponse: The app shows the in-order sequence before and after each rotation, so the student can see that it does not change.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why does a rotation never change the in-order sequence?

misconceptions.description: The student mixes up left and right rotations.
misconceptions.appResponse: The animation labels which node moves up and which moves down, and the captions say “Rotate C around G”.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: In a right rotation, which node moves up and which moves down?

misconceptions.description: The student uses a single rotation for an inside case (Case 2 or 3).
misconceptions.appResponse: An animation shows that a single rotation does not fix an inside case.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why does a single rotation not fix the inside cases?

misconceptions.description: The student does the two rotations of a double rotation in the wrong order, or about the wrong nodes.
misconceptions.appResponse: The worked example shows that the first rotation, about the child of n, turns Case 2 into Case 1.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: In a Left-Right double rotation, why is the first rotation about n.left?

misconceptions.description: The student confuses the inside and outside cases, and uses a double rotation where one rotation is enough.
misconceptions.appResponse: The case chart marks Cases 1 and 4 as outside cases and Cases 2 and 3 as inside cases.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: How can you tell from the path to the new key whether a case is inside or outside?

misconceptions.description: The student checks only the BST order, or only the balance, when verifying a tree after a rotation.
misconceptions.appResponse: The verification step always checks both the in-order sequence and every balance factor.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: What two properties must a tree satisfy after a rotation?

misconceptions.description: The student rebalances at the root or at the new node instead of at the first unbalanced node.
misconceptions.appResponse: The student answers “Click the node” questions, and the feedback highlights the path from the new key back up to the root.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why is rebalancing done at the first unbalanced node on the way up?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that an insertion may need rebalancing at several ancestors.
misconceptions.appResponse: A diagram shows that the fixed subtree has the same height as it had before the insertion.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why is one fix always enough after an insertion?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that a new key can be placed somewhere other than an empty leaf position, for example at the root.
misconceptions.appResponse: The insertion animation follows the search path down to an empty branch.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why does BST insertion always add the new key as a leaf?

misconceptions.description: The student goes right for a smaller key or left for a larger key.
misconceptions.appResponse: Each comparison has a caption that says whether the key is smaller or larger and which way the search goes.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Which way does a search go when the key is smaller than the node?

misconceptions.description: The student checks the BST rule only between a parent and its children, not for the whole subtree.
misconceptions.appResponse: The feedback points to the ancestor whose subtree contains the key.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why must every key in the left subtree be smaller than the node, not just the left child?

misconceptions.description: The student mixes up tree terms such as parent, child, sibling and leaf.
misconceptions.appResponse: The refresher labels the terms on a tree from the BST lectures.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Which tree terms do you want to check in the lecture?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that other nodes move when a leaf is removed.
misconceptions.appResponse: The deletion animation removes only the leaf before any balance check.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: What changes in the tree when a leaf is removed, before any rebalancing?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that deleting a leaf can never unbalance the tree.
misconceptions.appResponse: The opening example shows one leaf deletion that needs a rotation and one that does not.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: How can removing a leaf make an ancestor unbalanced?

misconceptions.description: The student updates only the parent's balance factor after a deletion.
misconceptions.appResponse: The animation updates the balance factors all the way up to the root.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: Why must balance factors be checked all the way up to the root after a deletion?

misconceptions.description: The student chooses an AVL tree even when the data is rarely searched by key or does not need to be kept in order.
misconceptions.appResponse: The scenario cards include cases, such as a log and a queue, where a simpler structure is better.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: When is a simpler structure a better choice than an AVL tree?

misconceptions.description: The student thinks that an AVL tree costs nothing extra compared with a plain BST.
misconceptions.appResponse: C8 lists the stored height and the rotation work as the price of guaranteed O(log n) search.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: What extra time and space does an AVL tree use, and when is it worth it?

misconceptions.description: The student prefers a structure with cheap updates even when searches far outnumber updates.
misconceptions.appResponse: The scenario cards state how often the data is searched and how often it changes.
misconceptions.lectureQuestion: How do you weigh search cost against update cost when choosing a structure?
